overview: Investore Property is an NZX-listed real estate investment trust that owns a $1.1 billion portfolio (43 properties, 31 March 2026) of convenience-based, large-format retail property in New Zealand, anchored predominantly by Woolworths NZ supermarkets and hardware retailers such as Bunnings and Mitre 10. The company is externally managed by Stride Investment Management Limited (SIML), part of the NZX-listed Stride Property Group, which is also Investore's 18.8% cornerstone shareholder. Investore is designated a 'Non-Standard' (NS) issuer by NZX because of this externally managed structure.

business_model.summary: Investore earns rental income from long-leased, non-discretionary 'everyday needs' retail property. Anchor tenants (Woolworths, Bunnings, Mitre 10, The Warehouse Group, Briscoes Group, Foodstuffs) provide ~81% of Contract Rental with structured (fixed/CPI) or turnover-linked rent reviews, while a growing base of mini-major and specialty tenants in multi-tenanted centres provides additional rental growth. Revenue is highly recurring (long WALT leases, 99.5% occupancy at FY26) rather than transactional; growth comes from rent reviews, developments/landlord capital contributions (rentalised at 6.5-7.5% yield on cost), and portfolio recycling (selling lower-growth assets, buying assets in key metro growth corridors).

revenue_streams.name: Woolworths NZ (supermarket) rent
revenue_streams.trend: declining share (was 84% at 2016 listing, actively diversified down)

revenue_streams.name: Other anchor tenants (Warehouse Group, Briscoes, Foodstuffs)

business_model.customer_type: B2B — commercial leases to large, listed/national retail tenants (not consumer-facing)
business_model.geographic_mix: North Island 87% (Auckland 50%, Wellington 12%, Waikato 8%, Bay of Plenty 2%, Other North Island 9%), South Island 13% (Canterbury & Otago 11%, Other South Island 2%), all New Zealand — Auckland exposure raised from 41% to 50% during FY26 via acquisitions

main_competitors: Stride Property Limited (SPL, sister diversified REIT)
direct unlisted/private LFR landlords and syndicators
competitive_position.market_position: One of New Zealand's largest dedicated large-format/convenience retail landlords and the primary NZX-listed pure-play in this sub-sector; scarce direct listed comparable given most NZX REITs are diversified (office/industrial/retail mix)

moat_factors.description: Well-located big-box/supermarket sites with adequate land, parking and site coverage in key metro growth corridors are difficult to replicate; large land holdings with low site coverage (e.g. 33% at Silverdale) provide future development optionality

moat_factors.factor: Tenant covenant quality and lease structure
moat_factors.description: Long WALT (5.9 years portfolio, 6.4 years for anchors) with nationally recognised, largely non-discretionary anchor tenants provides income certainty; structured/CPI/turnover-linked rent reviews embed contractual rental growth
Large-format retail generally has lower occupancy cost as a % of sales than mall/CBD retail, supporting tenant retention and renewal economics
43 properties, 186 tenants, growing mix of single- and multi-tenanted assets spreads risk versus a single-tenant landlord

weaknesses: Single-tenant concentration to Woolworths NZ remains very high (53% of Contract Rental at FY26, down from 62% pre-transactions and 84% at 2016 listing, but still dominant)
External management structure creates potential conflicts of interest, particularly around related-party transactions (e.g. FY26 Silverdale Centre acquisition from parent Stride Property Limited)
Small market capitalisation and constrained scale versus diversified REIT peers limits capital markets flexibility
Structurally geared balance sheet (LVR ~40%) makes NTA and earnings sensitive to interest rates and cap rates
Limited organic growth outside rent reviews — reliant on acquisitions/recycling for portfolio-level growth given a mature, largely full portfolio

growth_drivers: Structured/CPI and market rent reviews plus turnover-linked Woolworths rent embedding contractual like-for-like rental growth (4.7% like-for-like in FY26)
Portfolio recycling strategy — selling non-core/lower-growth assets at or above book value and redeploying into higher-growth, better-located metro assets (net +$125m recycled in HY26 alone)
Tenant-partnered capital works / landlord contributions (online fulfilment 'direct-to-boot' expansions at Woolworths stores) rentalised at attractive 6.5-7.5% yields on cost
Expanded investment mandate (approved at October 2025 Special Meeting) to include broader 'convenience-based retail' beyond traditional large-format retail, widening the acquisition pipeline
Falling OCR/interest rate cycle reducing cost of debt and potentially supporting cap rate stabilisation or compression, which would lift NTA and improve acquisition funding economics
Large, low-site-coverage landholdings offering future development/intensification optionality (e.g. Silverdale Centre at 33% site coverage)
Increasing multi-tenanted, mini-major/specialty exposure (up from 4% at listing to ~19% of Contract Rental) providing higher rental growth than single-tenant anchor leases

business.description: 53% of Contract Rental (down from 62% pre-FY26 transactions and 84% at listing) is derived from a single tenant group; any deterioration in Woolworths NZ's NZ retail strategy, store rationalisation, or credit quality would materially impact Investore's income

Shift to e-commerce/online grocery could reduce need for physical footprint over time, although Investore's tenants are increasingly using stores as fulfilment hubs (online expansion capex being funded by Investore itself, partially mitigating this)

SIML/Stride Property Group manages Investore and other Stride vehicles; the FY26 Silverdale Centre acquisition from parent Stride Property Limited (an 18.8% cornerstone shareholder) required a Special Meeting shareholder vote given its related-party nature — a structural governance issue that recurs whenever assets are traded between Stride entities

financial.description: LVR 40.1% at 31 March 2026 (covenant now ≤60% after being raised from 55%, board policy target 30-40%) — covenant was loosened for headroom, which itself signals rising leverage; further valuation declines or debt-funded acquisitions could pressure covenants

IPL020 ($NZ, 2.40% coupon) matures August 2027 and IPL030 (4.00% coupon) matures February 2027 — both are due to roll in FY2027 into what may be a higher-rate environment than their original coupons; company is proactively engaging lenders and monitoring bond markets
$62.5m subordinated convertible notes (6.25% coupon, 4-year, matures ~Sept 2029) can convert into ordinary shares, a potential source of future dilution alongside a relatively high funding cost
Net finance expense has risen from $14.0m (FY22) to $20.6m (FY26) as debt balances and rates increased, compressing the margin between net rental income growth and profit growth

regulatory.description: Requires NZX waivers from standard listing rules (2.2.1-2.8.1, 2.10.1) because of the externally managed structure — a persistent governance flag for some institutional investors

Transactions with Stride Property Limited/SIML require independent appraisal and shareholder approval processes (as seen with Silverdale Centre), adding execution risk/timing friction to related-party deals

macro.description: The dominant driver of reported results: the 2022-2023 OCR tightening cycle drove average portfolio capitalisation rates up ~130bp (from ~5.0% pre-cycle to a peak near 6.3%), causing investment property devaluations of $(185.3)m in FY23 and $(98.8)m in FY24 and cutting NTA per share from $2.32 (FY22) to $1.57 (FY24); a renewed rate-up cycle or cap rate re-expansion would again hit NTA and gearing
While anchor tenants are non-discretionary, mini-major and specialty tenants (19% of Contract Rental) and Woolworths turnover rent are more exposed to discretionary consumer spending cycles

FY26 annual report flags recent offshore geopolitical developments reintroducing inflation pressure and market uncertainty, likely slowing transactional activity and creating a more cautious near-term outlook

external_management.parent_group: NZX-listed Stride Property Group (Stride Property Limited/SPL + SIML, dual-listed/stapled structure)
external_management.fee_fy26: $8.0 million total management fees to SIML in FY26 (asset management fee $5.5m + other project/activity fees), up from $7.0m in FY25 (~$5.2m asset management fee), primarily due to higher total portfolio value and transaction/project activity
external_management.fee_structure_notes: Comprises a recurring asset management fee (broadly scales with portfolio value) plus activity-based fees tied to leasing, development and transaction activity; the FY26 Management Agreement amendments (approved at the October 2025 Special Meeting) also replaced a flat $10,000-per-property building management fee with a 'more equitable, market-aligned' structure and expanded Investore's investment mandate to include broader convenience-based retail
external_management.alignment_and_governance: Stride Property Limited holds an 18.8% cornerstone shareholding in Investore, partially aligning Stride Group economics with Investore shareholders, but SIML/SPL nominees also sit on the Investore Board (2 of ~5 directors — Ross Buckley and Tim Storey, who chairs Stride Property Limited and SIML) alongside independent directors. An independent review of SIML's management fees is conducted every two years, next due FY27. The FY26 Silverdale Centre acquisition — bought directly from parent Stride Property Limited — is the clearest recent illustration of the related-party conflict inherent in the structure; it required an independent appraisal and a shareholder vote at a Special Meeting, which shareholders approved in October 2025.
external_management.internalisation_debate: No formal internalisation proposal or takeover of the external manager is currently on foot as at August 2026. The external management structure remains a standing point of investor debate/scrutiny common to NZX externally-managed vehicles (cf. debates around other Stride Group entities and historical NZX manager-internalisation precedents at peers), but Investore's FY26 disclosures show the Board's response has been procedural (biennial independent fee reviews, fee-structure renegotiation, expanded mandate) rather than pursuing internalisation.

interest_rate_sensitivity.summary: Interest rates and cap rates are the dominant swing factor in Investore's reported results, given its 40%+ LVR and IFRS fair-value accounting for investment property.
interest_rate_sensitivity.ocr_cycle_impact: RBNZ OCR tightening from late 2021 through 2023 drove average portfolio capitalisation rates from the high-4%/low-5% range up to ~6.3%, producing investment property devaluations of $(185.3)m in FY23 and $(98.8)m in FY24 (loss after tax of $(150.2)m in FY23 and $(67.1)m in FY24) and cutting NTA per share from $2.32 (FY22) to $1.84 (FY23) to $1.57 (FY24). Cap rates and NTA have since stabilised/modestly recovered as the OCR cutting cycle progressed through 2025-2026: WACR was 6.3% at both 31 March 2025 and 31 March 2026, and NTA recovered to $1.60 (FY25) and $1.62 (FY26).
interest_rate_sensitivity.debt_and_hedging: Weighted average cost of debt was 4.2% at 31 March 2026 (up from 4.1% a year earlier, reflecting the convertible notes' fixed 6.25% coupon pulling the blended rate up even as underlying swap/bank rates fell). 80% of drawn debt (including convertible notes) was hedged/fixed as at 31 March 2026, up from 74% a year earlier. Weighted average fixed-rate maturity is short at ~1.9-2.4 years, meaning a meaningful portion of hedges roll and re-price within the DCF/investment horizon.
interest_rate_sensitivity.gearing_and_covenants: LVR 40.1% at 31 March 2026 (38.5% FY25), against a Board target policy of 30-40% and a bank covenant recently raised from ≤55% to ≤60% (providing headroom but also signalling rising leverage). Interest cover ratio improved to 3.3x (FY26) from 2.8x (FY25), covenant ≥1.75x.
interest_rate_sensitivity.debt_instruments: Bank debt facilities of $638m available/$515m drawn (pro forma, post the additional $100m Silverdale Centre facility) across a 6-bank syndicate (ANZ, CCB, ICBC, Westpac, CBA, Bank of China — two new lenders added FY26), with no bank debt maturing until FY30 after a $225m refinance/extension. Two listed retail bonds: IPL020 ($NZ, 2.40% coupon, matures 31 Aug 2027) and IPL030 (4.00% coupon, matures 25 Feb 2027) — both due to refinance in FY2027, likely at higher coupons than their original pricing. $62.5m subordinated convertible notes issued September 2025 (6.25% coupon, 4-year tenor to ~2029, convertible into ordinary shares at Investore's option at maturity), proceeds used to help fund the Silverdale Centre acquisition and repay bank debt.
interest_rate_sensitivity.outlook: Management (Chair's Letter, May 2026) explicitly frames the outlook as OCR-cut tailwind (lower funding costs, improved investor depth/liquidity for commercial property, 'inbound interest is strengthening') offset by renewed geopolitical/inflation risk creating near-term caution on transactional activity.

dividend_policy.policy: Investore's stated dividend policy is to distribute between 80% and 100% of Distributable Profit (a non-GAAP measure = profit before tax adjusted for non-recurring/non-cash items and current tax), paid quarterly.
dividend_policy.history_and_trend: FY26 cash dividend was 6.50 cents per share, in line with guidance, versus Distributable Profit per share of 8.13 cents (implying a payout ratio of ~80%, at the low end of policy). This compares with a higher dividend of 7.90 cents per share in FY23 despite similar or higher distributable profit per share in that year (8.44 cps FY23 vs 8.13 cps FY26) — i.e., the per-share cash dividend has been reduced by roughly 18% (7.90cps to 6.50cps) since FY23 even though underlying Distributable Profit per share has been broadly stable in the 7.6-8.4 cents range across FY22-FY26. The dividend reduction reflects Board caution on payout ratio and balance sheet conservatism through the higher interest rate/cap rate expansion period rather than a decline in underlying earnings power.
dividend_policy.sustainability: Distributable Profit (the basis for the payout policy) has been resilient and grew 8.1% in FY26 to $30.7m ($2.3m higher than FY25), supported by net rental income growth from acquisitions and rent reviews, comfortably covering the 6.50 cps FY26 dividend. Board has guided 6.50 cents per share again for FY27 (a 9.3% gross dividend yield on a 5-day VWAP basis per the Chair's Letter), signalling stability at the current lower payout level rather than further cuts or near-term increases.
dividend_policy.gaap_vs_distributable_profit_note: GAAP profit after tax is volatile and not representative of distributable capacity — it swung from a $150.2m loss (FY23) to a $67.1m loss (FY24) to profits of $38.4m (FY25) and $31.7m (FY26), almost entirely driven by non-cash investment property fair value movements, not the underlying rental business, which is why the company (and this analysis) anchors on Distributable Profit and AFFO rather than statutory NPAT.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ commercial property, including large-format retail, is entering a new cycle in 2026 as RBNZ OCR cuts through 2025-2026 (OCR down to ~2.25%) flow through to lower borrowing costs and improving investor depth/liquidity; cap rate compression is expected to be modest rather than dramatic given yield margins are already near long-term averages
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate — underlying rental income from non-discretionary anchor tenants is defensive and has proven resilient through the 2022-2024 downturn (net rental income grew every year FY22-FY26), but statutory earnings and NTA are highly cyclical due to mark-to-market cap rate/valuation swings
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High — both directly (variable-rate/refinancing debt cost, ~40% hedged floating exposure) and indirectly via cap rates driving investment property valuations and NTA; see interest_rate_sensitivity section above
key_input_costs: Construction and refurbishment costs for tenant capital works
Rates and property outgoings (largely recoverable from tenants under net leases)

recent_developments.event: FY26 annual result (year to 31 March 2026): net rental income $65.5m (+5.1%), Distributable Profit after tax $30.7m (+8.1%), Distributable Profit per share 8.13 cps (+7.3%), profit after tax $31.7m (down $6.6m YoY on a smaller valuation gain), NTA per share $1.62 (+$0.02), FY26 cash dividend 6.50 cps in line with guidance, FY27 dividend guidance reaffirmed at 6.50 cps
Portfolio valued at $1.1bn (+14%/$140m over 12 months), driven by the Silverdale Centre and Bunnings New Lynn acquisitions; LVR rose to 40.1% (from 38.5%) largely due to acquisition funding

Special Meeting of Shareholders: shareholders approved the related-party acquisition of Silverdale Centre from parent Stride Property Limited, the issue of $62.5m subordinated convertible notes (and deemed shares on conversion), and amendments to the Management Agreement with SIML (expanded mandate to convenience-based retail, revised building management fee structure)
Issued $62.5m four-year subordinated convertible notes (6.25% fixed coupon) via a retail offer to help fund the Silverdale Centre acquisition and repay bank debt

Acquired Bunnings New Lynn for $43m (6.1% initial yield) and Silverdale Centre, Auckland for $114m (6.8% initial yield); divested Woolworths Browns Bay and Woolworths New Brighton for a combined $31.8m, 5.2% above book value (5.9% blended initial yield) — net effect: reduced Woolworths concentration from 62% to 53% of Contract Rental and raised Auckland exposure from 41-42% to ~49-50%

Refinanced and extended $225m of bank debt facilities; added two new syndicate lenders (Commonwealth Bank of Australia NZ Branch, Bank of China Auckland Branch), taking the syndicate to six banks; no bank debt now matures before FY30; LVR covenant raised from ≤55% to ≤60% (Board policy target unchanged at 30-40%)

HY26 interim result (six months to 30 Sep 2025): profit after tax $12.8m (+$3.1m YoY), Distributable Profit per share 4.02 cps (+HY25's 3.73 cps), reaffirmed FY26 dividend guidance of 6.50 cps; LVR 34.2% at half-year (temporarily reduced by convertible note proceeds before further acquisition drawdown)

SIML total management fee income (across all Stride-managed vehicles) rose to $22.9m, up 12% from $20.4m in FY25, driven by growth in the Investore and Industre management arrangements; Investore-specific management fees to SIML were $8.0m in FY26, up from $7.0m in FY25

guidance.as_of: FY26 Annual Report / Chair's Letter, 21 May 2026

items.notes: Same as FY26 actual dividend; Board states this represents a 9.3% gross dividend yield assuming a 33% tax rate and the 5-day VWAP to 15 May 2026
Actual LVR was 40.1% at 31 March 2026, at the top of the target band; covenant separately raised from ≤55% to ≤60% for headroom

items.target: Proactively securing additional facilities / monitoring bond market for a possible new issuance
items.notes: No specific quantum or pricing guided; company says it has 'proactively engaged with its lenders regarding additional facility to fund these maturities'

items.target: Continue targeted recycling — selective disposals to reduce leverage and fund strategically aligned acquisitions
items.notes: No specific acquisition/disposal dollar targets given; qualitative commitment to 'proactive capital management' and portfolio optimisation continues

guidance.management_commentary: Chair Mike Allen: interest rates continuing to fall is improving investor depth and liquidity for commercial property and inbound interest is strengthening, but recent geopolitical tensions and rising energy costs have introduced a 'more cautious outlook' that is likely to slow transactional activity until there is greater clarity on costs and interest rates. The Board considers this point in the cycle still a good time to be active in the market and remains focused on executing the portfolio recycling strategy, while SIML (Manager's Report) similarly flags a likely slowdown in transactional activity near-term but reiterates confidence in the resilience of the non-discretionary, everyday-needs tenant base.

bull_case: Highly defensive, non-discretionary anchor tenant base (Woolworths NZ, Bunnings, Mitre 10) with 99.5% occupancy and long WALT (5.9 years portfolio, 6.4 years for anchors) provides resilient, largely contracted rental income through economic cycles

Falling OCR/interest rate cycle is a tailwind — reduces marginal funding costs, supports cap rate stabilisation/compression, and NTA has already recovered from the FY24 trough ($1.57) to $1.62 at FY26

Active, demonstrated portfolio recycling track record — FY26 divestments completed above book value (+5.2%) while acquisitions were made at attractive yields, evidencing genuine asset-selection skill by the manager and reducing single-tenant concentration over time (Woolworths down from 84% at listing to 53% at FY26)
Currently trades at a meaningful discount to NTA (~NZ$1.05 share price vs $1.62 NTA per share, a ~35% discount), offering potential re-rating upside if the discount narrows as rates stabilise

Attractive current dividend yield (~6.2% on the flat 6.50 cps FY27 guidance at NZ$1.05, ~9.3% gross including imputation per management's own disclosed calculation) with Distributable Profit comfortably covering the payout and growing (+8.1% in FY26)
bear_case: Persistent, high single-tenant concentration risk to Woolworths NZ (53% of Contract Rental) means Investore's fortunes are tightly linked to one counterparty's NZ store network and lease decisions, a risk not fully diversified away despite years of active reduction

External management by SIML/Stride Property Group creates ongoing governance friction and cost — FY26 management fees rose to $8.0m (+$1.0m YoY), and the FY26 Silverdale Centre purchase directly from the manager's own cornerstone shareholder (Stride Property Limited, 18.8% holder) is a textbook related-party conflict that required a special shareholder vote to approve

High interest-rate/cap-rate sensitivity already proven painful: FY23-FY24 saw a combined ~$250m of non-cash investment property devaluations and NTA fell from $2.32 to $1.57 per share; any reversal of the current rate-cutting cycle (e.g. from renewed inflation/geopolitical shocks, which management itself flags as a live risk) would likely repeat this dynamic

Dividend has already been cut materially from the cycle peak (7.90 cps FY23 to 6.50 cps FY26/27 guidance, roughly -18%) despite broadly stable underlying Distributable Profit per share, indicating Board conservatism/lower payout ratio rather than dividend growth as the near-term capital return story

Rising leverage and refinancing risk — LVR climbed to 40.1% (top of the 30-40% target band) after loosening the bank covenant from 55% to 60%, and two retail bonds (IPL020, IPL030) both mature in FY2027 requiring refinancing potentially at higher rates than their 2.40%/4.00% original coupons, on top of a relatively costly $62.5m convertible note tranche at 6.25%
